name: Next.js
summary: A React application framework that combines convention-based filesystem routing with server/client component boundaries, request handlers, and build output for multiple deployment modes.
scope: App Router route and layout conventions
React Server and Client Component boundary

features.name: Filesystem route-segment graph
features.description: In the App Router, folders define URL segments and convention files such as page, layout, loading, error, and route expose or compose route behavior; dynamic, grouped, parallel, and intercepted segments refine that graph.
benefits: Makes route structure visible in the source tree
Allows layouts and route segments to be composed by convention
costs: File naming and segment constraints become part of the application contract
The route graph must account for special-file conflicts and dynamic segments

features.name: Server/client component boundary
features.description: App Router layouts and pages are Server Components by default; a use-client boundary places a component and its imported module graph on the client, while server-rendered output and references form the React Server Component Payload used for hydration.
benefits: Keeps server-only data access and secrets out of the client module graph
Limits browser JavaScript to interactive subgraphs and supports progressive rendering
costs: Props crossing the boundary must satisfy serialization and composition constraints
Developers must reason about two execution environments and hydration

features.name: Web request/response route-handler adapter
features.description: A route.js/ts file defines Web Request/Response handlers for supported HTTP methods at an App Router segment; route handlers are distinct from page rendering at the same segment and can be configured for static or request-time behavior.
benefits: Provides an explicit API boundary beside UI routes
Uses standard Web request and response abstractions across supported runtimes
costs: A segment cannot expose page and route handlers in the same conflicting position
Caching and runtime behavior must be selected with route and data-fetching configuration

features.name: Render and cache deployment artifact
features.description: The framework analyzes route and data dependencies to prerender or render at request time, emits client/server assets and manifests, and provides deployment modes including Node.js and Docker self-hosting.
benefits: Permits static output where dependencies allow it while retaining dynamic routes
Packages routing and rendering metadata for a chosen deployment target
costs: Build output and cache behavior are coupled to runtime and configuration assumptions
Static/dynamic classification can change when request-time APIs or uncached data are introduced

mathematical_views.question: How do filesystem segments, special files, and dynamic parameters determine the public route set and nested layout composition?
assumptions: Folders and convention files are vertices or labels in a rooted tree
A public route exists only when a supported page or route convention is present
The view abstracts framework-specific route sorting and excludes undocumented deployment rewrites

mathematical_views.model: Two-environment component graph with serialized boundary
mathematical_views.question: Which component subgraphs execute on the server, which hydrate on the client, and what information crosses the boundary?
assumptions: Modules are vertices and imports/rendered-child relations are edges
use-client marks a client boundary and the RSC Payload is the boundary representation
The model abstracts React reconciliation and does not claim arbitrary props are serializable

mathematical_views.question: How does a route transition among build-time prerendering, request-time rendering, caching, and client hydration?
assumptions: A route state includes its data dependencies, cache policy, emitted payload, and runtime target
Documented request-time APIs and route configuration trigger transitions
This is an explanatory model rather than a proof of cache correctness or performance

costs: Topology is constrained by framework file conventions

benefits: Reduced client bundle and server-only data access
costs: Cross-environment composition and serialization add reasoning overhead
Route conflicts and cache/runtime configuration must be managed

benefits: One build can encode static and dynamic delivery choices
costs: Artifacts and cache semantics depend on deployment assumptions
